The California and US datasets were filtered into two other groups on the basis of the date they were published: period 1 (October 2021 to September 2022) and period 2 (October 2022 to October 2023), representing the pre‐ and post‐illegal laboratory establishment periods, respectively (Nguyen and Martin 2023). These two groups were plotted against each other in a time series over the course of a calendar year.To support the existence of geospatial variations of outbreak signals at the national and local levels, we implemented a hotspot analysis in the US to identify areas with statistically significant hotspots of outbreak signals within a 100‐km distance threshold. We used a 10‐km threshold in California to provide more granular context around the illegal laboratory, and respiratory pathogens can travel 10–18 km (Kersh et al. 2013). Therefore, a hotspot within 10 km of the illegal laboratory can provide suggestive evidence of aerosol pathogen leak from the lab. Significant hotspots indicate areas with a higher than expected number of outbreak signals, whereas cold spots denote areas with lower than expected outbreak signals within a 100‐km distance for the US. Getis–Ord Gi * statistics were used to identify areas with a higher risk or lower risk of outbreaks from 2021 to 2023 (Ord and Getis 2010). To identify significant spatial clustering of outbreaks in the US and California, the statistical analysis estimates Gi * using the following equation: (1) Gi∗=Σj=1nωijxj−x ̄Σj=1nωijSn∑j=1nωij2−∑j=1nωij2n−1 where ωij is the spatial weight between locations i and j, S and n are the standard deviation and the total number of attribute values xi, respectively, and x ̄ is the mean of xi. The Gi * value is classified on the basis of the outbreak signals in the US or California: hotspots (a higher number of signals than expected), cold spots (a lower number of signals than expected), and nonsignificant (with comparable numbers of observed and expected outbreak signals), based on 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence intervals (Ord and Getis 2010).
full_text_sections.results: 3ResultsWe identified 19,233 outbreak reports between October 1, 2021 and October 31, 2023. In the period after the establishment of the Reedley illegal laboratory in October 2022 (The Select Committee 2023; Nguyen and Martin 2023; Lopez 2023), reported outbreaks of pathogens associated with the illegal laboratory showed a slight increase in December 2022, June to August 2023, and October 2023 across the US (Figure 2). As shown by the red solid line in Figure 2, between June 2022 and August 2022 and from July 2023 to August 2023, reported outbreak signals involved a mix of illegal laboratory‐associated pathogens, including COVID‐19, malaria, dengue, hepatitis C, Escherichia coli, and respiratory syncytial virus. In the October 2023 peak, the reported outbreak signals also included a mix of pathogens, such as COVID‐19, dengue, E. coli, hepatitis B, herpes simplex, malaria, and respiratory syncytial virus.FIGURE 2Trends of monthly reports of outbreak signals in the United States from October 2021 to October 2023. Period one (from October 2021 to September 2022) refers to the period before the Reedley illegal laboratory began operation, and period two represents the period after the illegal laboratory started operating. The purple dashed line indicates the time when the laboratory began operation, and the red dashed vertical line indicates the time when the illegal laboratory closed.In California, outbreak reports of pathogens associated with the illegal laboratory (red line in Figure 3) show an increasing trend between August and November 2022, with a noticeable spike in December 2022. Other spikes occurred in April 2023 and August 2023. In contrast, the trends of pathogens not associated with illegal laboratory showed a decreasing pattern from August 2022 to January 2023 (see the light blue line in Figure 3).FIGURE 3Trends of monthly reports of outbreak signals in California from October 2021 to October 2023. Period one (from October 2021 to September 2022) refers to the period before the Reedley illegal laboratory began operation, and period two represents the period after the illegal laboratory started operating. The purple dashed line indicates the time when the laboratory began operation, and the red dashed vertical line indicates the time when the illegal laboratory closed.In the overall US hotspot analysis, California, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, central Florida, northern Michigan, Nebraska, New Hampshire, and central Alabama were identified as statistically significant hotspots. The distribution of outbreak signals in other states was not statistically significant and did not qualify as cold or hot spots (Figure 4).FIGURE 4Hotspot analysis of all outbreak signals within 100 km of threshold distance, data from EPIWATCH, 2021 to 2023.Figure 5 shows outbreak signal locations before (blue dots) and after (red dots) the Reedley illegal laboratory, along with their proximity to the illegal laboratory. The nearest outbreak signals from the Reedley illegal laboratory are ∼41 and 33 km away, before and after the illegal laboratory started operating, respectively (Figure 5).FIGURE 5Outbreak signals in California, data from EPIWATCH, 2021–2023.Figure 6 provides a polygon‐based optimized hotspot analysis to identify statistically significant hotspot areas of reported outbreak signals in California in a 10‐km radius. Statistically significant hotspots of outbreak signals were identified in San Francisco, Kern, and Los Angeles County, as displayed by the red polygons, whereas Fresno remains nonsignificant (Figure 6).FIGURE 6Optimized hotspot in California, within a 10‐km radius, data from EPIWATCH, 2021–2023.
full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThe failure to test samples found at the illegal laboratory in Reedley means there is considerable uncertainty about what pathogens were present and what impact these may have had on the surrounding community or environment. In the absence of any formal testing, reporting or data, but knowing that a staff member and their child became ill, we have shown that EPIWATCH can be used to analyze whether any unusual epidemic patterns were reported in the area. Changes in disease patterns reported in California or the US in the year following the establishment of the illegal laboratory may or may not be linked to the illegal laboratory. Some of the changes could be attributed to other factors. For instance, the increase in malaria reported in the southern US during the observation period may be attributable to other factors, such as climate change, coupled with vector movements (Bansal et al. 2023, Cui and Kim 2024). The October 2023 increase in reports of disease due to pathogens associated with the laboratory is temporally related to locally acquired cases of dengue being reported in California in late 2023 (California Department of Public Health 2025, Sutter‐Yuba Mosquito and Vector Control District 2025). Dengue was one of the apparent samples in the lab, but locally acquired dengue has also been reported in California since 2013, and the vector, Aedes aegypti, is present in California (Gloria‐Soria et al. 2014, California Department of Public Health (n.d.). Early warning systems, such as EPIWATCH, have the potential to detect unusual outbreaks of infectious disease much sooner than traditional surveillance methods, and when formal data are unavailable (MacIntyre et al. 2022, 2023, Hutchinson et al. 2023). The availability of open‐source data does not depend on whether a laboratory incident has been formally reported to domestic or international authorities.Laboratory accidents and laboratory‐acquired infections can occur even in well‐regulated and controlled situations (Duizer et al. 2023; Casassus 2021; Pappas 2022). The risk may be greater in unregulated laboratories. Given the known occurrence of laboratory‐acquired infections in legitimate laboratories (Dhawan et al. 2025), we can assume that they may also occur in clandestine laboratories.The report from the US Select Committee on the CCP mentioned that the person caring for the laboratory mice in the illegal laboratory and his child were sick (The Select Committee 2023). Such infections may be directly linked to contact with infected mice or samples and may serve as an index case for community‐level outbreaks.Historically, similar incidents associated with pathogens have had political or personal economic influences (MacIntyre 2023; Culp 2013; Engells 2013). The owner of the Reedley illegal laboratory had alleged ties with the Chinese military (Rumpf‐Whitten 2023). In the context of escalating geopolitical tension between the US and China, the Reedley illegal laboratory raises concerns of espionage, biological smuggling, or even the intent to conduct a Trojan Horse attack (MacIntyre 2023). The owner is a fugitive wanted by the Canadian government, who moved to the US illegally, changed his name, rebranded test kits and biological materials bought in China, sold them as made in the US, and finally was receiving payments from the Chinese government (The Select Committee 2023; U.S. FDA 2023; Nava 2023; Jeunesse and Ross 2024; Morrison 2023). In 2026, a further illegal lab also connected to this individual was identified in Las Vegas, with reports of people becoming ill (Charns 2026). This highlights the ongoing threat and the lack of tools or systems to identify or mitigate illegal labs. Tools, such as EPIWATCH, can provide early warnings of unusual epidemics, which may signal illegal biolabs.Globally, no oversight regulation for illegal laboratories. Biosafety and biosecurity guidelines in the US target legal biosafety laboratories in research institutions, universities, and pharmaceutical companies; none for illegals (Kuiken 2024). These regulatory frameworks have no clear borders, creating overlapping responsibilities (Kuiken 2024; Howell 2026). The Reedley illegal laboratory was detected accidentally. Following the initial identification of the illegal laboratory, it took over 3 months to be granted an inspection warrant (December 2022 to March 16, 2023), and over 6 months had elapsed to secure an abatement warrant (December 2022 to June 26, 2023) (The Select Committee 2023; Willis 2023). In addition, investigations conducted by organizations, such as the CDC, were delayed and insufficient (see Table A1). Such delays can increase the public health risks to the community.Investigating and responding to biosecurity threats require coordinated action by public health organizations (e.g., CDC and NIH), law enforcement groups, and the public. The US FBI is the leading organization to prepare and respond to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear threats of weapons of mass destruction (Federal Bureau of Investigation). Therefore, the FBI is expected to lead the detection and testing of unknown biological and chemical samples, like the Reedley, in collaboration with the CDC, NIH, and the public. However, the FBI closed its investigation shortly and stated, “they believe there were no materials that posed a potential weapons of mass destruction threat” to the city (The Select Committee 2023). Neither the CDC nor the FBI tested the samples.These delays and the inadequate response may reflect a lack of regulatory oversight, creating uncertainty about what to do, when, and which organization is responsible for which action. The Reedley lab samples were discarded without testing; the lack of frameworks may be the reason, as was the case when the Reedley illegal laboratory was identified in late 2022. However, another illegal lab was identified in early 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The FBI collected samples and sent them for testing (Howell 2026), but it did not publicly report the findings. After the Reedley illegal laboratory identification, legislation was developed in 2025 to incorporate bans on illegal laboratories and governance‐related measures (Buckley 2024; Willis 2024; Costa 2025), which may help the FBI and other organizations become more alert and responsible in investigating such events in Las Vegas (Cortez Masto 2026).
full_text_sections.conclusion: 6ConclusionIn a situation, such as the Reedley laboratory, where authorities failed to test or investigate adequately, open‐source intelligence may be useful in independently assessing whether any animal or human outbreaks may have been associated with the laboratory. This remains a possibility but cannot be proven in the absence of formal testing and reporting. Formal surveillance data from California public health authorities could be analyzed in a similar way to our study, which would provide validated results.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionPrivate laboratories, facilities owned, controlled, or operated by private nongovernmental organizations, are increasing in number and are difficult to regulate and monitor, with the possibility of unauthorized activity, which can pose a public health threat through accidental or deliberate release (Terrell 2023; Fidler and Gostin 2020; MacIntyre 2023; McDade and Franz 1998; Casagrande et al. 2023). A report by Gryphon Scientific highlighted the sheer volume of private sector research involving human pathogens across the United States (US), noting that the private sector performs a large proportion of life science research with dual‐use potential without proper oversight (Casagrande et al. 2023). The private sector pathogen research community may be legitimate on the whole, but bad actors may exist within it and may seek to utilize these “invisible” laboratories for intentional, malicious acts (Greene et al. 2024). In addition to known private sector laboratories, there is a risk of illegal, undocumented laboratories, such as the one found in Reedley, California (Bari and MacIntyre 2025).The 1984 Rajneesh incident in the US, state of Oregon, is an example of the threat of clandestine laboratories. In the privacy of a 64,000‐acre ranch owned by the Rajneesh Movement, cult members created an undocumented and illegal laboratory where they cultured a range of pathogens, including Salmonella typhimurium (MacIntyre 2015). Cult members intentionally contaminated 10 restaurant salad bars across the county with this pathogen as a beta test, resulting in at least 751 cases. The final attack was to be contamination of the city water supply prior to a local election. Their goal was to incapacitate county voters and sway the outcome of county elections, seize control of local government, and overcome restrictions placed on them for land development (McDade and Franz 1998). Public health authorities incorrectly declared this a natural epidemic caused by poor hygiene. It would be nearly a year before the Rajneesh laboratory was discovered by accident, and more than a decade before the public narrative was revised to state that this was a biological attack (MacIntyre 2023).The Reedley incident has demonstrated the ease with which illegal laboratories can operate undetected, and the lack of systems or processes for identifying such threats (MacIntyre 2023). The illegal laboratory was operational from October 2022. In late December 2022, a local code officer noticed a hose coming out of a previously abandoned warehouse in Reedley, California, and raised the alarm. This building had been rewired and rebuilt in breach of established building codes and housed complex laboratory equipment. Almost 1000 humanized transgenic mice were found in inhumane conditions, with 200 of these found dead and disposed of inappropriately in general waste streams (The Select Committee 2023).In 2023, following expressions of concern from both Republican and Democratic Members of Congress, a report on the Reedley incident was drafted by the United States Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Reviewing a substantial body of evidence, “the report identified that a wanted fugitive” (and a national of the People's Republic of China) was responsible for establishing and operating this illegal facility. The report also determined that the laboratory was able to purchase the resources and pathogens entirely from US laboratories, but that no monitoring of the purchase or sale of these substances currently exists (The Select Committee 2023). In their closing statements, the Select Committee noted that as of December 2023, it was unknown whether other laboratories similar to the one found in Reedley existed elsewhere within the US (The Select Committee 2023, Rodriguez 2023). There is no systematic method for identifying undocumented laboratories, nor has this been a focus of intelligence agencies. The Reedley illegal laboratory owner had ties with the Chinese government (Rumpf‐Whitten 2023). The owner changed his name, used a false identity in the US (U.S. FDA 2023), and had been involved in a number of fraudulent acts. These included misbranding of test kits bought in China, relabeled as made in the US, and resold as a new brand (The Select Committee 2023; Rumpf‐Whitten 2023; U.S. Attorney's Office Eastern District of California 2023; Nava 2023).Although documented high‐containment biolabs are regulated, oversight of private laboratories is almost nonexistent (The Select Committee 2023; United States Government Accountability Office 2023). Further, illegal laboratories are not systematically considered or searched for. Legitimate laboratories in the US are expected to be overseen by the CDC or the federal government if they have research funded by the federal government (The Select Committee 2023; United States Government Accountability Office 2023). Those laboratories funded by the private sector are not overseen nor expected to report to the CDC or Federal agencies. The Reedley illegal laboratory falls outside of both these categories. Both the CDC and the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) initially refused the local authorities’ request to investigate, and when they did, vials labeled with the names of dangerous pathogens, which should be handled in BSL‐4 laboratories, including “Ebola,” were destroyed rather than tested (The Select Committee 2023). This fragmented system and lack of accountability create dangerous loopholes that allow for the operation of undocumented and “invisible” laboratories whose biosafety and biosecurity standards rely upon self‐policing. Ultimately, scientists with private funding may conduct unsupervised research with pathogens that could cause outbreaks, severe illness, and death (Greene et al. 2024).Uncovering public health threats linked with illegal biological research is difficult and may be protracted. For instance, the 1984 Rajneesh Salmonella incident was dismissed by health authorities as a natural outbreak and not correctly identified as bioterrorism until a year later (MacIntyre 2015). Public officials initially declared that the Salmonella outbreak was linked to poor hygiene in salad bars and closed multiple restaurants in response to the outbreak (MacIntyre 2015). The investigation of the current Reedley illegal laboratory was also delayed and inadequate for timely detection. The CDC responded to the situation 5 months later, on May 2, 2023, and completed a review in 2 days, by May 4, 2023, during which 20 potentially infectious agents were discovered. The CDC reported that the laboratory didn't have select agent pathogens, despite failing to test any samples (Greene et al. 2024) (Table 1). A vial labeled Ebola was found on the premises, a select agent pathogen that should be handled in BSL‐4 laboratories (The Select Committee 2023; Nava 2023). Overall, thousands of vials of potentially infectious agents were seized and destroyed without being tested (The Select Committee 2023). The national security threat and true intent of this facility may never be known. analysis.methods: The spatial pattern of outbreak signals was analyzed using hotspot analysis, and the distances of outbreak signals from the laboratory were measured. The availability of open-source data does not depend on whether a laboratory incident has been formally reported to domestic or international authorities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: In the absence of any formal testing, reporting or data, but knowing that a staff member and their child became ill, we have shown that EPIWATCH can be used to analyze whether any unusual epidemic patterns were reported in the area. analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to estimate epidemic signals around the Reedley illegal laboratory using open-source epidemic intelligence data. It analyzed the spatial patterns of outbreak signals and compared trends of pathogens associated with the illegal laboratory to those not associated. The results showed that 33.3% of outbreak signals were country-level reports, while 41.5% were more granular. There was a slight increase in outbreaks of pathogens linked to the illegal laboratory in specific months, and the nearest outbreak signals were approximately 41 and 33 km away. However, the study acknowledges that the observed changes in disease patterns may not be directly linked to the illegal laboratory. The findings highlight the potential of EPIWATCH for early detection of unusual outbreaks, even in the absence of formal data. The study's limitations include the lack of formal testing and the possibility of other factors influencing the reported disease patterns.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 这项研究旨在利用开源流行病情报数据来估计里德利非法实验室周围的流行病信​​号。Gi * 值根据美国或加利福尼亚州的 暴发 信号进行分类:热点(信号数量高于预期)、冷点(信号数量低于预期)和不显着(观察到的和预期的 暴发 信号数量相当),基于 90%、95% 和 99% 置信区间(Ord 和 Getis 2010)。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用了对 2021 年 10 月至 2023 年 10 月加州和美国开源流行病情报数据的地理空间分析。搜索词包括里德利非法实验室提到的所有可能的病原体(特别委员会 2023;Nava 2023)。
elements_zh.methods: 使用热点分析对暴发信号的空间模式进行分析,并测量暴发信号与实验室的距离。使用 R tidyverse 软件包和 MS Excel 进行数据管理、处理和清理;图表是使用 ggplot 制作的,地图是使用 ArcGIS 制作的。我们分析了非法实验室中记录的病原体的趋势,以及美国和加利福尼亚州非法实验室中未记录的病原体的趋势,以比较每个类别内部和之间的趋势。
elements_zh.main_results: 在研究期间报告的 19,233 个 暴发 信号中,33.3% 是没有州级位置数据的国家级报告,25.2% 是州级报告,41.5% 比州级更精细(图 1)。在2022年10月里德利非法实验室成立后的一段时间内,全美报告的与该非法实验室相关的病原体暴发在2022年12月、2023年6月至2023年8月和2023年10月略有增加(图2)。在非法实验室开始运营之前和之后,距离 Reedley 非法实验室最近的 暴发 信号分别为 41 公里和 33 公里(图 5)。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to estimate epidemic signals around the Reedley illegal laboratory using open-source epidemic intelligence data. The Gi * value is classified on the basis of the outbreak signals in the US or California: hotspots (a higher number of signals than expected), cold spots (a lower number of signals than expected), and nonsignificant (with comparable numbers of observed and expected outbreak signals), based on 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence intervals (Ord and Getis 2010).
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study used geospatial analysis of open-source epidemic intelligence data for California and the US from October 2021 to October 2023. Search terms included all possible pathogens mentioned at the Reedley illegal laboratory (The Select Committee 2023; Nava 2023).
analysis_en.methods: The spatial pattern of outbreak signals was analyzed using hotspot analysis, and the distances of outbreak signals from the laboratory were measured. Data curation, processing, and cleaning utilized R tidyverse packages and MS Excel; graphs were made using ggplot, and maps were made using ArcGIS. We analyzed the trends of pathogens documented in the illegal laboratory, along with those not documented in the illegal laboratory in the US and California, to compare trends within and across each category.
analysis_en.main_results: Of the 19,233 outbreak signals reported in the study period, 33.3% were country-level reports without state-level location data, 25.2% were state-level reports, and 41.5% were finer than the state level (Figure 1). In the period after the establishment of the Reedley illegal laboratory in October 2022, reported outbreaks of pathogens associated with the illegal laboratory showed a slight increase in December 2022, June to August 2023, and October 2023 across the US (Figure 2). The nearest outbreak signals from the Reedley illegal laboratory are ∼41 and 33 km away, before and after the illegal laboratory started operating, respectively (Figure 5).
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The October 2023 increase in reports of disease due to pathogens associated with the laboratory is temporally related to locally acquired cases of dengue being reported in California in late 2023 (California Department of Public Health 2025, Sutter-Yuba Mosquito and Vector Control District 2025). Changes in disease patterns reported in California or the US in the year following the establishment of the illegal laboratory may or may not be linked to the illegal laboratory.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Early warning systems, such as EPIWATCH, have the potential to detect unusual outbreaks of infectious disease much sooner than traditional surveillance methods, and when formal data are unavailable. The availability of open-source data does not depend on whether a laboratory incident has been formally reported to domestic or international authorities.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: In the absence of any formal testing, reporting or data, but knowing that a staff member and their child became ill, we have shown that EPIWATCH can be used to analyze whether any unusual epidemic patterns were reported in the area. The supplied evidence does not report any formal testing or data to confirm a causal link between the illegal laboratory and the observed disease patterns.

papers.title: Respiratory pathogens detected by multiplex PCR in Malaysian public hospitals: prevalence and epidemiologic patterns from January 2023 until July 2024.
papers.abstract: Respiratory tract infections remain an important cause of hospitalisation and diagnostic uncertainty, and multiplex polymerase chain reaction testing offers rapid detection of multiple pathogens in routine clinical practice. We aimed to describe the prevalence, demographic associations, and temporal trends of respiratory pathogens detected by the QIAstat-Dx Respiratory SARS-CoV-2 Panel in Malaysian public hospitals. This multicentre retrospective cross-sectional study included nasopharyngeal swab samples from cases with suspected acute respiratory infections tested between 1 January 2023 and 31 July 2024. Data were collected from participating sites using standardised record forms and analysed. We assessed overall positivity, pathogen frequencies, age-group and regional distributions, and monthly and quarterly trends. A total of 8,361 samples were included, of which 5,252 (62.8%) had at least one pathogen detected. Single detections were identified in 4,279 samples (51.2%), while co-detections were observed in 973 samples (11.6%). Viral pathogens predominated. Rhinovirus/enterovirus was the most frequently detected pathogen (23.8%), followed by respiratory syncytial virus A/B (13.7%) and influenza A H1N1/2009 (4.8%). Positivity was highest among children aged 1 to 4 years and infants aged 1 to 11 months, and age-related variation was more pronounced than regional variation. The leading pathogens also demonstrated distinct temporal profiles, with different peak months across the study period. In conclusion, respiratory pathogen detection in this hospital-based population was characterised by a high positivity rate, predominance of viral pathogens, marked age-related differences, and distinct temporal patterns. These findings support the value of multiplex PCR for respiratory pathogen surveillance in Malaysian public hospitals.

papers.title_zh: 马来西亚公立医院通过多重 PCR 检测到的呼吸道病原体:患病率 和 2023 年 1 月至 2024 年 7 月的流行病学模式。
papers.source_body_en: Respiratory tract infections remain an important cause of hospitalisation and diagnostic uncertainty, and multiplex polymerase chain reaction testing offers rapid detection of multiple pathogens in routine clinical practice. We aimed to describe the prevalence, demographic associations, and temporal trends of respiratory pathogens detected by the QIAstat-Dx Respiratory SARS-CoV-2 Panel in Malaysian public hospitals. This multicentre retrospective cross-sectional study included nasopharyngeal swab samples from cases with suspected acute respiratory infections tested between 1 January 2023 and 31 July 2024. Data were collected from participating sites using standardised record forms and analysed. We assessed overall positivity, pathogen frequencies, age-group and regional distributions, and monthly and quarterly trends. A total of 8,361 samples were included, of which 5,252 (62.8%) had at least one pathogen detected. Single detections were identified in 4,279 samples (51.2%), while co-detections were observed in 973 samples (11.6%). Viral pathogens predominated. Rhinovirus/enterovirus was the most frequently detected pathogen (23.8%), followed by respiratory syncytial virus A/B (13.7%) and influenza A H1N1/2009 (4.8%). Positivity was highest among children aged 1 to 4 years and infants aged 1 to 11 months, and age-related variation was more pronounced than regional variation. The leading pathogens also demonstrated distinct temporal profiles, with different peak months across the study period. In conclusion, respiratory pathogen detection in this hospital-based population was characterised by a high positivity rate, predominance of viral pathogens, marked age-related differences, and distinct temporal patterns. These findings support the value of multiplex PCR for respiratory pathogen surveillance in Malaysian public hospitals.
papers.abstract_zh: 呼吸道感染仍然是住院和诊断不确定性的重要原因,多重聚合酶链反应检测可以在常规临床实践中快速检测多种病原体。我们的目的是描述马来西亚公立医院 QIAstat-Dx 呼吸道 SARS-CoV-2 检测组检测到的呼吸道病原体的 患病率、人口统计学关联和时间趋势。这项多中心回顾性横断面研究包括 2023 年 1 月 1 日至 2024 年 7 月 31 日期间检测的疑似急性呼吸道感染病例的鼻咽拭子样本。使用标准化记录表格从参与地点收集数据并进行分析。我们评估了总体阳性率、病原体频率、年龄组和区域分布以及月度和季度趋势。共纳入 8,361 个样本,其中 5,252 个样本(62.8%)至少检测到一种病原体。在 4,279 个样本 (51.2%) 中发现了单一检测,而在 973 个样本 (11.6%) 中发现了联合检测。病毒病原体占主导地位。鼻病毒/肠道病毒是最常检测到的病原体(23.8%),其次是呼吸道合胞病毒 A/B(13.7%)和甲型H1N1/2009流感(4.8%)。1至4岁儿童和1至11个月婴儿的阳性率最高,且与年龄相关的差异比区域差异更明显。主要病原体还表现出不同的时间特征,在整个研究期间具有不同的高峰月份。总之,该医院人群的呼吸道病原体检测具有阳性率高、病毒病原体占主导地位、明显的年龄相关差异和不同的时间模式的特点。这些研究结果支持了马来西亚公立医院呼吸道病原体 监测 多重 PCR 的价值。

papers.title: A digitalized nosocomial risk management framework during the COVID-19 pandemic: practice-based insights from a tertiary cancer hospital in Southwest China

source_records.title: A digitalized nosocomial risk management framework during the COVID-19 pandemic: practice-based insights from a tertiary cancer hospital in Southwest China

papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: BackgroundCancer patients represent a particularly vulnerable population during infectious disease outbreaks, with substantially elevated risk of infection and mortality compared to the general population. Comprehensive nosocomial risk management frameworks for specialized oncology hospitals remain under-documented in the literature.MethodsThis community case study describes a comprehensive, multi-component epidemic risk management program implemented at Sichuan Cancer Hospital—the largest tertiary cancer hospital in Southwest China—from January 2020 to September 2022. The program integrated seven management pillars with a digital risk-reporting pipeline built on Questionnaire Star® and R programming language.ResultsOver the 32-month study period, the hospital achieved a 98% staff vaccination rate with 95% booster coverage. Following its deployment in August 2022, during the final weeks of the study period, the digital reporting system processed risk-investigation data and generated actionable summary tables within 5 min of submission. No nosocomial COVID-19 cases were detected among patients or staff during the surveillance period.ConclusionThe experience demonstrates that systematic integration of management innovations with digital technologies can support hospital infection prevention even under extreme epidemiological pressure; the absence of detected nosocomial cases, however, cannot be causally attributed to the program alone given concurrent community-level restrictions. The framework’s pathogen-agnostic architecture supports transferability to future respiratory virus epidemics in cancer hospital settings. 7Acknowledgment of conceptual and methodological constraintsThis study is subject to the following conceptual and methodological constraints: (1) the single-center design limits generalizability; findings should be validated in multi-center studies across diverse institutional and regulatory contexts. (2) The observational nature precludes causal attribution of the absence of detected nosocomial cases to specific program components. (3) The Zero-COVID policy period during which the program operated confounds the estimation of standalone program effectiveness. (4) Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections may have been undetected due to the absence of systematic asymptomatic screening. (5) The 32-month observation window does not capture the complete post-pandemic transition, and longer-term sustainability assessments are needed. (6) The digital pipeline’s performance was evaluated during a single hospital’s operations; scalability to multi-hospital networks remains untested. (7) Because systematic asymptomatic screening was not performed throughout the study period, the reported outcome refers to detected cases only. 5DiscussionThis community case study describes a comprehensive nosocomial epidemic risk management program implemented at a large tertiary cancer hospital during the COVID-19 pandemic, yielding three principal findings: (1) the systematic integration of management innovations with digital technologies can function as a force multiplier for infection prevention; (2) the framework’s core architecture is pathogen-agnostic and transferable to future epidemic scenarios; and (3) no nosocomial COVID-19 cases were detected over 32 months despite repeated community outbreaks, a finding best interpreted as an association between the program and the absence of detected cases rather than proof of causation.5.1Integration of management and technology as a force multiplierThe program’s key innovation lies not in any single component but in the systematic integration of management strategies with digital technologies. The seven management pillars—leadership accountability, zoned-tiered prevention, epidemiological intelligence, grid-based supervision, network-based training, vaccination campaigns, and the digital pipeline (Table 1)—are individually well-documented in the infection prevention literature (11, 22–24), but their combined, mutually reinforcing implementation has not been described in a cancer hospital context. The digital pipeline in particular served as the informational backbone of the framework, enabling the rapid translation of raw risk-investigation data into actionable intelligence that directly informed management decisions. This finding aligns with recent systematic reviews showing that hospitals employing integrated, multi-component infection prevention bundles achieve superior outcomes compared to those implementing isolated interventions (24, 25). Layered multimodal quality-improvement initiatives have likewise demonstrated measurable reductions in device-associated infections in intensive care settings (26), further supporting the value of integrated rather than isolated interventions.5.2Transferability beyond COVID-19Although the program was developed and tested in the COVID-19 context, its core architecture is pathogen-agnostic. The structured data-capture templates in Questionnaire Star® can be rapidly reconfigured for other infectious disease threats (e.g., influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, or novel respiratory pathogens) by modifying the field set without altering the R processing logic. The R script’s modular design allows the addition of new data validation rules and the generation of pathogen-specific summary tables with minimal reprogramming. International equivalents of the data-capture platform [REDCap, Qualtrics, Google Forms (20)] and the platform-agnostic nature of the R back end (which accepts any structured CSV or Excel input) facilitate cross-border replication. This flexibility is particularly relevant given the increasing recognition that future respiratory virus epidemics are inevitable and that healthcare systems must maintain “warm” surveillance infrastructure between outbreaks (27, 28).5.3Comparison with published literatureThe existing literature on COVID-19 infection prevention and control in oncology settings can be broadly categorized into three groups: (a) clinical outcome studies reporting infection rates and mortality among cancer patients (5–9, 29); (b) expert commentaries and guideline documents providing management recommendations (10, 30–33); and (c) technology-focused reports on specific tools such as telehealth or health informatics systems (11, 14, 15). The present study contributes to a fourth, under-represented category: structured, practice-based descriptions of integrated frameworks that combine organizational and technological components into a coherent whole. Recent publications have emphasized the importance of such integrated approaches for post-pandemic preparedness (25–27), but detailed implementation accounts from specialized cancer hospitals remain limited. The R-based automated processing pipeline described here extends the existing literature on digital surveillance tools (15, 16, 25) by demonstrating a low-cost, platform-agnostic solution that does not require proprietary hospital information system integration.5.4Practical challenges and recommendationsSeveral challenges encountered during program implementation warrant discussion. First, information interoperability between medical institutions remains a systemic barrier: different hospitals in the same region used incompatible reporting systems, preventing cross-institutional risk data sharing. This limitation could be addressed through the adoption of standardized data exchange formats (e.g., HL7 FHIR) at the policy level. Second, the reliance on Questionnaire Star® as a commercial platform introduces a vendor-dependency risk; the platform-agnostic design described in Section 3.2.1 provides a mitigation strategy. Third, the initial configuration of the 17-field form required multiple iterations to balance comprehensiveness with completion time—a consideration for institutions developing similar tools. Finally, staff compliance with daily risk-reporting was initially suboptimal and required targeted communication campaigns and integration of reporting status into departmental performance metrics.5.5LimitationsThis report has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, as a single-center case study, the generalizability of the findings to other institutional contexts—particularly hospitals with different resource levels, regulatory environments, or patient populations—requires further validation through multi-center replication studies. Second, the program was implemented during China’s “Zero-COVID” policy period, which included community-level non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) such as lockdowns, mass testing, and travel restrictions. The observed absence of detected nosocomial cases reflects the combined effect of the hospital’s internal program and external community-level NPIs; isolating the independent contribution of the hospital’s program is not possible from this observational data. Future studies conducted in settings without concurrent community-level restrictions would help estimate the program’s standalone effectiveness. Third, asymptomatic infections may have gone undetected, as routine asymptomatic screening of all staff and patients was not systematically performed during the entire study period. Fourth, the 32-month observation window, while capturing multiple epidemic waves, does not include the full post-pandemic transition period. Finally, this report is observational in nature and was not designed as a controlled intervention study with a comparator group.5.6Interaction with community-level Zero-COVID policyAn important interpretative consideration is the interaction between the hospital’s internal program and China’s national Zero-COVID policy, which was active during the entire study period. Community-level non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs)—including city-wide lockdowns during the August 2022 Chengdu outbreak, universal masking mandates, mass PCR testing, and inter-city travel restrictions—undoubtedly reduced the baseline risk of SARS-CoV-2 introduction into the hospital. However, several observations are consistent with a contribution of the hospital’s internal program to the absence of detected nosocomial cases. First, the hospital continued to receive patients from across Sichuan and neighboring provinces throughout the study period, including from regions with active community transmission, because cancer treatment cannot be indefinitely deferred. Second, the August 2022 Chengdu outbreak occurred despite existing community-level NPIs, indicating that community measures alone could not completely eliminate importation risk. Third, the digital pipeline was activated specifically in response to the failure of manual reporting channels during this outbreak, and the rapid availability of risk-stratified data directly enabled the leadership group to implement targeted, rather than blanket, staff deployment decisions—suggesting that the program may have added value beyond what community measures alone could provide. A cautious interpretation is therefore that the absence of detected nosocomial cases represents the combined effect of community-level NPIs and the hospital’s internal framework, with each component addressing different points in the transmission chain.5.7Post-study implementation example: influenza preparedness (2023–2024)Following the lifting of Zero-COVID restrictions in December 2022, and outside the stated study window (January 2020–September 2022), the hospital repurposed the digital risk-reporting pipeline for the 2023–2024 influenza season. The Questionnaire Star® form was reconfigured within 48 h by replacing COVID-19-specific fields (health code status, nucleic acid test results) with influenza-specific fields (influenza vaccination status, antiviral prophylaxis, symptom checklist), while preserving the demographic and contact-tracing fields. The R script required modification to only the variable-labeling module (approximately 20 lines of code), with the core data-cleaning, deduplication, and summary-table-generation logic remaining unchanged. This post-study implementation example demonstrates the framework’s operational flexibility and illustrates the feasibility of adapting the pathogen-agnostic architecture described in Section 5.2 to a different respiratory pathogen. full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundCancer patients represent a particularly vulnerable population during infectious disease outbreaks, with substantially elevated risk of infection and mortality compared to the general population. Comprehensive nosocomial risk management frameworks for specialized oncology hospitals remain under-documented in the literature.MethodsThis community case study describes a comprehensive, multi-component epidemic risk management program implemented at Sichuan Cancer Hospital—the largest tertiary cancer hospital in Southwest China—from January 2020 to September 2022. The program integrated seven management pillars with a digital risk-reporting pipeline built on Questionnaire Star® and R programming language.ResultsOver the 32-month study period, the hospital achieved a 98% staff vaccination rate with 95% booster coverage. Following its deployment in August 2022, during the final weeks of the study period, the digital reporting system processed risk-investigation data and generated actionable summary tables within 5 min of submission. No nosocomial COVID-19 cases were detected among patients or staff during the surveillance period.ConclusionThe experience demonstrates that systematic integration of management innovations with digital technologies can support hospital infection prevention even under extreme epidemiological pressure; the absence of detected nosocomial cases, however, cannot be causally attributed to the program alone given concurrent community-level restrictions. The framework’s pathogen-agnostic architecture supports transferability to future respiratory virus epidemics in cancer hospital settings.
full_text_sections.methods: 7Acknowledgment of conceptual and methodological constraintsThis study is subject to the following conceptual and methodological constraints: (1) the single-center design limits generalizability; findings should be validated in multi-center studies across diverse institutional and regulatory contexts. (2) The observational nature precludes causal attribution of the absence of detected nosocomial cases to specific program components. (3) The Zero-COVID policy period during which the program operated confounds the estimation of standalone program effectiveness. (4) Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections may have been undetected due to the absence of systematic asymptomatic screening. (5) The 32-month observation window does not capture the complete post-pandemic transition, and longer-term sustainability assessments are needed. (6) The digital pipeline’s performance was evaluated during a single hospital’s operations; scalability to multi-hospital networks remains untested. (7) Because systematic asymptomatic screening was not performed throughout the study period, the reported outcome refers to detected cases only.
full_text_sections.discussion: 5DiscussionThis community case study describes a comprehensive nosocomial epidemic risk management program implemented at a large tertiary cancer hospital during the COVID-19 pandemic, yielding three principal findings: (1) the systematic integration of management innovations with digital technologies can function as a force multiplier for infection prevention; (2) the framework’s core architecture is pathogen-agnostic and transferable to future epidemic scenarios; and (3) no nosocomial COVID-19 cases were detected over 32 months despite repeated community outbreaks, a finding best interpreted as an association between the program and the absence of detected cases rather than proof of causation.5.1Integration of management and technology as a force multiplierThe program’s key innovation lies not in any single component but in the systematic integration of management strategies with digital technologies. The seven management pillars—leadership accountability, zoned-tiered prevention, epidemiological intelligence, grid-based supervision, network-based training, vaccination campaigns, and the digital pipeline (Table 1)—are individually well-documented in the infection prevention literature (11, 22–24), but their combined, mutually reinforcing implementation has not been described in a cancer hospital context. The digital pipeline in particular served as the informational backbone of the framework, enabling the rapid translation of raw risk-investigation data into actionable intelligence that directly informed management decisions. This finding aligns with recent systematic reviews showing that hospitals employing integrated, multi-component infection prevention bundles achieve superior outcomes compared to those implementing isolated interventions (24, 25). Layered multimodal quality-improvement initiatives have likewise demonstrated measurable reductions in device-associated infections in intensive care settings (26), further supporting the value of integrated rather than isolated interventions.5.2Transferability beyond COVID-19Although the program was developed and tested in the COVID-19 context, its core architecture is pathogen-agnostic. The structured data-capture templates in Questionnaire Star® can be rapidly reconfigured for other infectious disease threats (e.g., influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, or novel respiratory pathogens) by modifying the field set without altering the R processing logic. The R script’s modular design allows the addition of new data validation rules and the generation of pathogen-specific summary tables with minimal reprogramming. International equivalents of the data-capture platform [REDCap, Qualtrics, Google Forms (20)] and the platform-agnostic nature of the R back end (which accepts any structured CSV or Excel input) facilitate cross-border replication. This flexibility is particularly relevant given the increasing recognition that future respiratory virus epidemics are inevitable and that healthcare systems must maintain “warm” surveillance infrastructure between outbreaks (27, 28).5.3Comparison with published literatureThe existing literature on COVID-19 infection prevention and control in oncology settings can be broadly categorized into three groups: (a) clinical outcome studies reporting infection rates and mortality among cancer patients (5–9, 29); (b) expert commentaries and guideline documents providing management recommendations (10, 30–33); and (c) technology-focused reports on specific tools such as telehealth or health informatics systems (11, 14, 15). The present study contributes to a fourth, under-represented category: structured, practice-based descriptions of integrated frameworks that combine organizational and technological components into a coherent whole. Recent publications have emphasized the importance of such integrated approaches for post-pandemic preparedness (25–27), but detailed implementation accounts from specialized cancer hospitals remain limited. The R-based automated processing pipeline described here extends the existing literature on digital surveillance tools (15, 16, 25) by demonstrating a low-cost, platform-agnostic solution that does not require proprietary hospital information system integration.5.4Practical challenges and recommendationsSeveral challenges encountered during program implementation warrant discussion. First, information interoperability between medical institutions remains a systemic barrier: different hospitals in the same region used incompatible reporting systems, preventing cross-institutional risk data sharing. This limitation could be addressed through the adoption of standardized data exchange formats (e.g., HL7 FHIR) at the policy level. Second, the reliance on Questionnaire Star® as a commercial platform introduces a vendor-dependency risk; the platform-agnostic design described in Section 3.2.1 provides a mitigation strategy. Third, the initial configuration of the 17-field form required multiple iterations to balance comprehensiveness with completion time—a consideration for institutions developing similar tools. Finally, staff compliance with daily risk-reporting was initially suboptimal and required targeted communication campaigns and integration of reporting status into departmental performance metrics.5.5LimitationsThis report has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, as a single-center case study, the generalizability of the findings to other institutional contexts—particularly hospitals with different resource levels, regulatory environments, or patient populations—requires further validation through multi-center replication studies. Second, the program was implemented during China’s “Zero-COVID” policy period, which included community-level non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) such as lockdowns, mass testing, and travel restrictions. The observed absence of detected nosocomial cases reflects the combined effect of the hospital’s internal program and external community-level NPIs; isolating the independent contribution of the hospital’s program is not possible from this observational data. Future studies conducted in settings without concurrent community-level restrictions would help estimate the program’s standalone effectiveness. Third, asymptomatic infections may have gone undetected, as routine asymptomatic screening of all staff and patients was not systematically performed during the entire study period. Fourth, the 32-month observation window, while capturing multiple epidemic waves, does not include the full post-pandemic transition period. Finally, this report is observational in nature and was not designed as a controlled intervention study with a comparator group.5.6Interaction with community-level Zero-COVID policyAn important interpretative consideration is the interaction between the hospital’s internal program and China’s national Zero-COVID policy, which was active during the entire study period. Community-level non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs)—including city-wide lockdowns during the August 2022 Chengdu outbreak, universal masking mandates, mass PCR testing, and inter-city travel restrictions—undoubtedly reduced the baseline risk of SARS-CoV-2 introduction into the hospital. However, several observations are consistent with a contribution of the hospital’s internal program to the absence of detected nosocomial cases. First, the hospital continued to receive patients from across Sichuan and neighboring provinces throughout the study period, including from regions with active community transmission, because cancer treatment cannot be indefinitely deferred. Second, the August 2022 Chengdu outbreak occurred despite existing community-level NPIs, indicating that community measures alone could not completely eliminate importation risk. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a digitalized nosocomial risk management framework in preventing SARS-CoV-2 transmission within a tertiary cancer hospital during the COVID-19 pandemic, given the heightened vulnerability of cancer patients to infection and mortality.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a single-center case study conducted at a tertiary cancer hospital in Southwest China over a 32-month period, focusing on the implementation of a digitalized risk management program during the national Zero-COVID policy period.
analysis.methods: The program utilized a digital risk-reporting pipeline built on Questionnaire Star® and R programming language, incorporating systematic integration of management strategies with digital technologies, and relied on community-level non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) such as lockdowns, mass testing, and travel restrictions.
analysis.main_results: Over the 32-month study period, the hospital achieved a 98% staff vaccination rate with 95% booster coverage. No nosocomial COVID-19 cases were detected among patients or staff during the surveillance period. The program was reconfigured within 48 hours to address other infectious diseases such as influenza.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the absence of detected nosocomial cases as an association rather than proof of causation, noting that the program's effectiveness may have been influenced by concurrent community-level restrictions. The novelty lies in demonstrating the utility of integrated, multi-component infection prevention strategies using digital tools.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that systematic integration of management innovations with digital technologies can support hospital infection prevention during outbreaks, particularly in high-risk settings like cancer hospitals, and highlight the importance of such frameworks for post-pandemic preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its single-center design, which restricts generalizability, and the concurrent community-level restrictions that may have confounded the assessment of the program's standalone effectiveness. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates a digitalized nosocomial risk management framework implemented at a tertiary cancer hospital in Southwest China during the COVID-19 pandemic. The framework integrated management strategies with digital technologies, including a Questionnaire Star®-based surveillance system and R programming language. Over 32 months, the hospital achieved a high staff vaccination rate and did not detect any nosocomial COVID-19 cases, despite repeated community outbreaks. The authors interpret these results as an association rather than proof of causation, given the concurrent national Zero-COVID policy. The study highlights the potential of integrated, multi-component infection prevention strategies for high-risk settings and post-pandemic preparedness. However, its single-center design limits generalizability, and further multi-center studies are needed to validate the framework's effectiveness. The findings suggest that digital tools can support hospital infection prevention, but their standalone impact remains unclear due to overlapping public health measures.

papers.source_body_en: Comprehensive nosocomial risk management frameworks for specialized oncology hospitals remain under-documented in the literature.MethodsThis community case study describes a comprehensive, multi-component epidemic risk management program implemented at Sichuan Cancer Hospital—the largest tertiary cancer hospital in Southwest China—from January 2020 to September 2022. The program integrated seven management pillars with a digital risk-reporting pipeline built on Questionnaire Star® and R programming language.ResultsOver the 32-month study period, the hospital achieved a 98% staff vaccination rate with 95% booster coverage. Following its deployment in August 2022, during the final weeks of the study period, the digital reporting system processed risk-investigation data and generated actionable summary tables within 5 min of submission. 7Acknowledgment of conceptual and methodological constraintsThis study is subject to the following conceptual and methodological constraints: (1) the single-center design limits generalizability; findings should be validated in multi-center studies across diverse institutional and regulatory contexts. (7) Because systematic asymptomatic screening was not performed throughout the study period, the reported outcome refers to detected cases only. BackgroundCancer patients represent a particularly vulnerable population during infectious disease outbreaks, with substantially elevated risk of infection and mortality compared to the general population. No nosocomial COVID-19 cases were detected among patients or staff during the surveillance period.ConclusionThe experience demonstrates that systematic integration of management innovations with digital technologies can support hospital infection prevention even under extreme epidemiological pressu...
papers.abstract_zh: 文献中对肿瘤专科医院的综合院内风险管理框架的记录仍然不足。方法本社区案例研究描述了中国西南最大的三级肿瘤医院四川省肿瘤医院(中国西南最大的三级癌症医院)从 2020 年 1 月至 2022 年 9 月实施的一项全面的、多组成部分的流行病风险管理项目。该项目将七个管理支柱与基于 Questionnaire Star® 和 R 编程语言构建的数字风险报告管道集成在一起。结果在 32 个月的研究期间,该医院实现了 98% 的员工 疫苗接种 率和 95% 的助推器覆盖率。继 2022 年 8 月部署后,在研究期的最后几周,数字报告系统处理了风险调查数据,并在提交后 5 分钟内生成了可操作的汇总表。7 承认概念和方法上的限制本研究受到以下概念和方法上的限制:(1)单中心设计限制了普遍性;研究结果应在不同机构和监管背景下的多中心研究中得到验证。(7)由于整个研究期间没有进行系统的无症状筛查,因此报告的结果仅指发现的病例。背景癌症患者是传染病 暴发 期间特别脆弱的人群,与一般人群相比,感染和 暴发 的风险显着升高。监测期间,患者或工作人员中没有发现院内COVID-19病例。结论经验表明,即使在极端的流行病学压力下,管理创新与数字技术的系统整合也可以支持医院感染预防。
papers.summary_zh: 文献中对肿瘤专科医院的综合院内风险管理框架的记录仍然不足。方法本社区案例研究描述了中国西南最大的三级肿瘤医院四川省肿瘤医院(中国西南最大的三级癌症医院)从 2020 年 1 月至 2022 年 9 月实施的一项全面的、多组成部分的流行病风险管理项目。该项目将七个管理支柱与基于 Questionnaire Star® 和 R 编程语言构建的数字风险报告管道集成在一起。结果在 32 个月的研究期间,该医院实现了 98% 的员工 疫苗接种 率和 95% 的助推器覆盖率。继 2022 年 8 月部署后,在研究期的最后几周,数字报告系统处理了风险调查数据,并在提交后 5 分钟内生成了可操作的汇总表。7 承认概念和方法上的限制本研究受到以下概念和方法上的限制:(1)单中心设计限制了普遍性;研究结果应在不同机构和监管背景下的多中心研究中得到验证。(7)由于整个研究期间没有进行系统的无症状筛查,因此报告的结果仅指发现的病例。背景癌症患者是传染病 暴发 期间特别脆弱的人群,与一般人群相比,感染和 暴发 的风险显着升高。监测期间,患者或工作人员中没有发现院内COVID-19病例。结论经验表明,即使在极端的流行病学压力下,管理创新与数字技术的系统整合也可以支持医院感染预防。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估在 COVID-19 大流行期间,数字化医院风险管理框架在三级癌症医院内预防 SARS-CoV-2 传播 的有效性,因为癌症患者对感染和 死亡率 的脆弱性更高。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是在中国西南地区一家三级肿瘤医院进行的为期 32 个月的单中心案例研究,重点关注国家“零新冠”政策期间数字化风险管理计划的实施情况。
analysis_zh.methods: 该计划利用基于 Questionnaire Star® 和 R 编程语言构建的数字风险报告管道,将管理策略与数字技术系统集成,并依靠社区层面的非药物干预措施 (NPI),例如封锁、大规模检测和旅行限制。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在 32 个月的研究期间,医院实现了 98% 的员工 疫苗接种 率和 95% 的加强覆盖率。监测 期间,在患者或工作人员中未发现院内 COVID-19 病例。该计划在 48 小时内进行了重新配置,以应对流感等其他传染病。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将未发现院内病例解释为一种关联,而不是因果关系的证据,并指出该计划的有效性可能受到同时存在的社区层面限制的影响。新颖之处在于使用数字工具展示集成的、多成分的感染预防策略的实用性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,管理创新与数字技术的系统整合可以支持 暴发 期间的医院感染预防,特别是在癌症医院等高风险环境中,并强调了此类框架对于大流行后准备的重要性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到单中心设计的限制,限制了普遍性,并且同时存在的社区层面的限制可能会混淆对该项目独立有效性的评估。由于这些限制,证据是中等的。

Send Close Pediatric Infections Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on X Email Article Copy Article Url Print OCTOBER 23, 2026 IDWeek 2026 RSV-B Lineage Emerges as Standout in Severe Pediatric Disease By Anna Tsioulias Young children infected with certain respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) subgroup B lineages experienced greater disease severity than those infected with RSV-A, according to a study presented at IDWeek 2026, in Washington, D.C. Source: Adobe. The biggest potential culprit? RSV-B lineage B.D.E.1. Related Content RSV Vaccination Shows Effectiveness at Year 3 A new study has found that vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains effective three years ... This Year’s U.S. Measles Cases Soar Beyond 4,000 The United States has identified 4,080 confirmed measles cases in 2026, as of CDC data updated on Oct. 8. Starting HPV Vaccine at Age 9 or 10 Raises Series Completion by 13 Starting the HPV vaccine series younger substantially increased the share of children who began and finished the ... The findings shed new light on a longstanding debate regarding the relative virulence of RSV antigenic subgroups. Although both RSV-A and RSV-B are established players in severe pediatric respiratory disease, prior studies have yielded conflicting results on whether differences in viral glycoproteins, including the fusion (F) and attachment (G) proteins, influence clinical severity. “We actually initially thought RSV-A was more pathogenic than RSV-B,” explained Kim El Haddad, MD, a pediatric infectious diseases physician at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, in Washington, D.C. “These new findings help clarify with very statistically significant results that the lineage B was associated with worse outcomes, although the fact that this study had more RSV-B than RSV-A cases (216 vs. 129) might affect precision.” In a prospective study spanning seven respiratory seasons (2015-2021), investigators at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, in Memphis, Tennessee, collected nasal swabs from 345 previously healthy children younger than 2 years of age: 22% with mild (outpatient) and 78% with moderate to severe (inpatient) RSV infection. After whole-genome sequencing, significant differences emerged across six RSV lineages with regard to disease severity scores (P=0.01), pediatric ICU admissions (P<0.0001), duration of oxygen supplementation (P=0.04), oxygen delivery methods (P<0.0001), and hospital length of stay (P=0.03). B.D.E.1 (n=61) was associated with particularly severe clinical outcomes, with nearly three-fourths of infected children requiring PICU admission. However, Dr. El Haddad, who was not involved with the research, noted that the changing distribution of RSV lineages across respiratory seasons could complicate interpretation, especially considering disruptions in viral circulation during the COVID-19 pandemic. “During peak COVID times, isolation measures created what we call an immunity debt, as many children were not exposed to RSV,” Dr. El Haddad told Infectious Disease Special Edition. “When restrictions eased in 2021, we saw a surge in B.D.E.1 infections. I wonder whether this lack of previous exposure contributed to a stronger inflammatory response with elevated cytokine levels and ultimately more severe disease. “I would also be interested in knowing whether viral loads differed between RSV-A and RSV-B infections, as reflected by cycle threshold values. A higher viral burden could contribute to both the more pronounced inflammatory response and greater disease severity observed with certain RSV-B lineages.” Looking beyond differences in clinical severity, the investigators uncovered distinct genomic and inflammatory profiles among RSV subgroups. More specifically, RSV-B showed greater sequence variability across F, G, and M2-2 proteins, raising questions about potential implications for RSV immunoprophylaxis. Dr. El Haddad noted that nirsevimab (Beyfortus, Sanofi/AstraZeneca) and clesrovimab (Enflonsia, Merck) target the F protein, but whether the observed genetic variation influences monoclonal antibody effectiveness remains unknown; however, she considered a clinically meaningful impact unlikely. RSV-B infections were also linked with a more pronounced mucosal inflammatory response, with age-adjusted analyses identifying 22 cytokines at significantly higher concentrations than in RSV-A infections (P<0.01). These cytokines formed two distinct clusters: one involving innate immune activation and interleukin-1 signaling, the other with chemotaxis and cellular stress pathways. Of importance, previous RSV exposure and the associated immune response could potentially affect cytokine profiles and disease severity during subsequent infections, according to Dr. El Haddad. “As the authors didn’t mention it, I am interested to know whether any children had prior RSV infections. If prior infection was not accounted for, it could represent a potential confounder.” Dr. El Haddad reported no relevant financial disclosures. Britannica Editors Last updated Oct. 26, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything News • Cranking up a natural defense pathway boosts cells' resistance to RSV • Oct. 20, 2026, 12:40 PM ET (Medical Xpress) ...(Show more) 3 viruses are more active in California in the fall. How to identify symptoms • Oct. 9, 2026, 12:00 PM ET (The Sacramento Bee) Show less respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), infectious agent of the respiratory system that typically produces a mild coldlike illness but in susceptible individuals, particularly infants under six months of age, is a major cause of severe and potentially fatal lower respiratory disease. Severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) occurs most commonly in the elderly and in young children. An estimated 60 to 70 percent of children have been infected with RSV by age one, and nearly all children have been infected by age two. Because RSV effectively evades immunity, repeat infections are common. RSV infection is seasonal, occurring as an annual epidemic during the winter in most countries in temperate regions. What's the Difference Between Bacteria and Viruses?Knowing the difference isn't just a technical distinction—it can save lives.(more) See all videos for this article Direct person-to-person contact is thought to be the most common route of RSV transmission. The virus also can be transmitted through the air, such as by coughing or sneezing, and through direct contact with a contaminated surface followed by touching of the face. Symptoms generally appear within four to six days of infection and include runny nose, cough, sore throat, headache, fever, and wheezing. In instances of severe illness, affected individuals may have a high fever, severe wheezing, rapid or laboured breathing, and bluish lips or fingers. Infants may only show signs of irritability, fatigue, and breathing difficulties, even in severe cases. The only pharmacological therapy available for treatment of RSV is the nucleoside analogue ribavirin, which can be administered orally, parenterally (by injection or infusion), or by inhalation. An injectable humanized monoclonal antibody is available for prevention of severe RSV illness in high-risk infants and children. It provides passive immunity and must by given by intramuscular injection once a month during RSV season. Transmission can be prevented with frequent handwashing, cleaning of surfaces, avoiding close contact with others, and covering the mouth and nose with the upper arm when coughing or sneezing. It provides passive immunity and must by given by intramuscular injection once a month during RSV season. Transmission can be prevented with frequent handwashing, cleaning of surfaces, avoiding close contact with others, and covering the mouth and nose with the upper arm when coughing or sneezing. news.content_title: Enanta Pharmaceuticals Announces First Patient Dosed in the RESOLVE Phase 2b/3 Study of Zelicapavir, a Potential First-in-Disease Treatment for Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) – Company Announcement - FT.com
news.content: Global Phase 2b/3 Study Will Evaluate Symptom Duration and Hospitalization Rates in Adult Outpatients at High Risk of Severe Outcomes from RSV Topline Phase 2b Data Expected in 2027 WATERTOWN, Mass. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 26, 2026-- Enanta Pharmaceuticals , Inc. (NASDAQ:ENTA), a clinical-stage biotechnology company dedicated to creating small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases, today announced that the first patient has been dosed in RESOLVE, its global Phase 2b/3 clinical trial of zelicapavir in adults at high risk of severe outcomes from RSV infection. Topline data from the Phase 2b portion of the study are expected in 2027. “We are excited to advance our zelicapavir program into a Phase 2b/3 study with the dosing of the first patient in RESOLVE,” said Scott T. Rottinghaus , M.D., Chief Medical Officer of Enanta Pharmaceuticals . “Based on learnings from our Phase 2 RSVHR study, the RESOLVE trial is enrolling adults at high risk for severe outcomes from RSV. These patients with congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or age of 75 or older have substantial disease burden and the potential to benefit from an RSV treatment. The Phase 2b portion is designed to confirm the treatment effect size and generate an additional dataset with the goal of strengthening the clinical evidence supporting zelicapavir. Together with LOTUS, our pediatric Phase 2b trial, this progress positions us to deliver two important Phase 2b data readouts in 2027 and marks a significant step forward in the development of zelicapavir. With no approved RSV antiviral therapies currently available, these advancements underscore the potential for zelicapavir to become a first-in-disease antiviral treatment.” "RSV remains a significant cause of illness, particularly among older adults and individuals with underlying health conditions who are at heightened risk of severe disease. Despite RSV’s burden, there are no treatment options available,” said Juan Antonio Carmona Herrera , M.D., a Principal Investigator in the RESOLVE study and President of C&A Clinical Trials Corp. “An effective antiviral has the potential to change the way RSV is managed by directly targeting the virus, with the goal of reducing disease severity, preventing complications, and improving patient outcomes. The development of a treatment specifically for RSV would represent an important advancement for physicians and the millions of patients at risk of serious illness each year." The Phase 2b/3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter global trial will evaluate the efficacy and safety of zelicapavir in adult outpatients who test positive for RSV and have had respiratory tract infection symptoms for no more than 3 days. Patients will have at least one of the following risk factors: 75 years of age or older, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or congestive heart failure. These risk factors are the same as the HR3 population in the Company’s previous Phase 2 RSVHR trial where a one-week reduction in time to complete resolution of symptoms, as well as a reduction in hospitalization, were observed. Patients will receive an oral dose of 800mg of zelicapavir or placebo once daily for 7 days and be evaluated for 28 days thereafter. The primary endpoint is the time to complete resolution of all 13 RSV symptoms as measured by the RiiQTM tool. A key secondary endpoint will evaluate hospitalization rate, with other secondary endpoints of additional clinical efficacy measures, antiviral activity, and safety of zelicapavir. The Phase 2b portion of the study will include a minimum of 200 patients and is designed to confirm the treatment effect size on the primary and key secondary endpoints in the targeted population, while the Phase 3 portion of the study is expected to enroll approximately 660 patients. About Zelicapavir Zelicapavir is being developed for the treatment of RSV infection and has been granted Fast Track designation by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration . Zelicapavir inhibits the RSV N-protein with nanomolar activity against both RSV-A and RSV-B. This mechanism is differentiated from RSV fusion inhibitors as targeting the N-protein inhibits viral replication versus viral entry and has a high barrier to resistance. In a Phase 2 trial of hospitalized and non-hospitalized pediatric RSV patients aged 28 days to 3 years old, zelicapavir demonstrated an antiviral effect and shortened time to complete resolution of RSV symptoms. In a Phase 2 trial of high-risk adults, a clinically meaningful improvement in time to complete resolution of all 13 RSV symptoms was observed for zelicapavir compared to placebo, with a benefit of 6.7 days for patients with congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or age 75 years or older, termed the HR3 population. Importantly, zelicapavir treatment resulted in a lower hospitalization rate, with an RSV-related hospitalization rate of 5% in placebo, compared to 0% in patients who received zelicapavir. Throughout its clinical development program, zelicapavir has demonstrated a favorable safety profile and has been well-tolerated in more than 700 people to date. About RSV RSV is the most common cause of bronchiolitis (inflammation of the small airways in the lung) and pneumonia in children under one year of age in the United States and a significant cause of respiratory illness in older adults and immunocompromised individuals. 1,2 According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , virtually all children in the United States get an RSV infection by the time they are two years old. 3 RSV represents a significant health threat for adults older than 50 years of age, with up to 180,000 hospitalizations associated with RSV infections annually in the United States . 2 Overall, in the United States , RSV accounts for up to 6.8 million outpatient visits and approximately 370,000 hospitalizations, with 24,000 deaths. 4 About Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. Enanta is using its robust, chemistry-driven approach and drug discovery capabilities to become a leader in the discovery and development of small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases. In virology, Enanta’s clinical programs are focused on the development of first-in-disease and best-in-disease treatments for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The Company’s immunology pipeline aims to develop treatments for inflammatory diseases by targeting key drivers of the type 2 immune response, with KIT, STAT6 and MRGPRX2 inhibition. Glecaprevir, a protease inhibitor discovered by Enanta, is part of the only treatment approved for curing both acute and chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and is sold by AbbVie in numerous countries under the tradenames MAVYRET® (U.S.) and MAVIRET® (ex-U.S.) (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir). A portion of Enanta’s royalties from HCV products developed under its collaboration with AbbVie contribute ongoing funding to Enanta’s operations. Please visit www.enanta.com for more information. Forward Looking Statements This press release contains forward-looking statements, including statements with respect to the Phase 2b/3 study of zelicapavir and the timeline and prospects for advancement of zelicapavir for the treatment of RSV. Statements that are not historical facts are based on management’s current expectations, estimates, forecasts and projections about Enanta’s business and the industry in which it operates and management’s beliefs and assumptions. The statements contained in this release are not guarantees of future performance and involve certain risks, uncertainties and assumptions, which are difficult to predict. Therefore, actual outcomes and results may differ materially from what is expressed in such forward-looking statements. Important factors and risks that may affect actual results include: clinical drug development involves a lengthy and expensive process with uncertain timelines and uncertain outcomes, the Phase 2b portion of Enanta’s Phase 2b/3 trial of zelicapavir for RSV may not support the Phase 3 portion, Enanta’s clinical trials, including its Phase 2b/3 trial, may fail to demonstrate sufficient safety and efficacy and, if that occurs, it may be unable to commercialize its product candidates on a timely basis or ever, the impact of development, regulatory and marketing efforts of others with respect to vaccines and competitive treatments for RSV; the discovery and development risks of Enanta’s programs in virology and immunology; Enanta’s limited clinical development experience; Enanta’s ability to partner its RSV or other programs; Enanta’s need to attract and retain senior management and key research and development personnel; Enanta’s need to obtain and maintain patent protection for its product candidates and avoid potential infringement of the intellectual property rights of others; and other risk factors described or referred to in “Risk Factors” in Enanta’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year-ended September 30, 2025, as updated by periodic reports subsequently filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Enanta cautions investors not to place undue reliance on the forward-looking statements contained in this release. These statements speak only as of the date of this release, and Enanta undertakes no obligation to update or revise these statements, except as may be required by law. References 1.
