news.content_original: Global Phase 2b/3 Study Will Evaluate Symptom Duration and Hospitalization Rates in Adult Outpatients at High Risk of Severe Outcomes from RSV Topline Phase 2b Data Expected in 2027 WATERTOWN, Mass. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 26, 2026-- Enanta Pharmaceuticals , Inc. (NASDAQ:ENTA), a clinical-stage biotechnology company dedicated to creating small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases, today announced that the first patient has been dosed in RESOLVE, its global Phase 2b/3 clinical trial of zelicapavir in adults at high risk of severe outcomes from RSV infection. Topline data from the Phase 2b portion of the study are expected in 2027. “We are excited to advance our zelicapavir program into a Phase 2b/3 study with the dosing of the first patient in RESOLVE,” said Scott T. Rottinghaus , M.D., Chief Medical Officer of Enanta Pharmaceuticals . “Based on learnings from our Phase 2 RSVHR study, the RESOLVE trial is enrolling adults at high risk for severe outcomes from RSV. These patients with congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or age of 75 or older have substantial disease burden and the potential to benefit from an RSV treatment. The Phase 2b portion is designed to confirm the treatment effect size and generate an additional dataset with the goal of strengthening the clinical evidence supporting zelicapavir. Together with LOTUS, our pediatric Phase 2b trial, this progress positions us to deliver two important Phase 2b data readouts in 2027 and marks a significant step forward in the development of zelicapavir. With no approved RSV antiviral therapies currently available, these advancements underscore the potential for zelicapavir to become a first-in-disease antiviral treatment.” "RSV remains a significant cause of illness, particularly among older adults and individuals with underlying health conditions who are at heightened risk of severe disease. Despite RSV’s burden, there are no treatment options available,” said Juan Antonio Carmona Herrera , M.D., a Principal Investigator in the RESOLVE study and President of C&A Clinical Trials Corp. “An effective antiviral has the potential to change the way RSV is managed by directly targeting the virus, with the goal of reducing disease severity, preventing complications, and improving patient outcomes. The development of a treatment specifically for RSV would represent an important advancement for physicians and the millions of patients at risk of serious illness each year." The Phase 2b/3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter global trial will evaluate the efficacy and safety of zelicapavir in adult outpatients who test positive for RSV and have had respiratory tract infection symptoms for no more than 3 days. Patients will have at least one of the following risk factors: 75 years of age or older, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or congestive heart failure. These risk factors are the same as the HR3 population in the Company’s previous Phase 2 RSVHR trial where a one-week reduction in time to complete resolution of symptoms, as well as a reduction in hospitalization, were observed. Patients will receive an oral dose of 800mg of zelicapavir or placebo once daily for 7 days and be evaluated for 28 days thereafter. The primary endpoint is the time to complete resolution of all 13 RSV symptoms as measured by the RiiQTM tool. A key secondary endpoint will evaluate hospitalization rate, with other secondary endpoints of additional clinical efficacy measures, antiviral activity, and safety of zelicapavir. The Phase 2b portion of the study will include a minimum of 200 patients and is designed to confirm the treatment effect size on the primary and key secondary endpoints in the targeted population, while the Phase 3 portion of the study is expected to enroll approximately 660 patients. About Zelicapavir Zelicapavir is being developed for the treatment of RSV infection and has been granted Fast Track designation by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration . Zelicapavir inhibits the RSV N-protein with nanomolar activity against both RSV-A and RSV-B. This mechanism is differentiated from RSV fusion inhibitors as targeting the N-protein inhibits viral replication versus viral entry and has a high barrier to resistance. In a Phase 2 trial of hospitalized and non-hospitalized pediatric RSV patients aged 28 days to 3 years old, zelicapavir demonstrated an antiviral effect and shortened time to complete resolution of RSV symptoms. In a Phase 2 trial of high-risk adults, a clinically meaningful improvement in time to complete resolution of all 13 RSV symptoms was observed for zelicapavir compared to placebo, with a benefit of 6.7 days for patients with congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or age 75 years or older, termed the HR3 population. Importantly, zelicapavir treatment resulted in a lower hospitalization rate, with an RSV-related hospitalization rate of 5% in placebo, compared to 0% in patients who received zelicapavir. Throughout its clinical development program, zelicapavir has demonstrated a favorable safety profile and has been well-tolerated in more than 700 people to date. About RSV RSV is the most common cause of bronchiolitis (inflammation of the small airways in the lung) and pneumonia in children under one year of age in the United States and a significant cause of respiratory illness in older adults and immunocompromised individuals. 1,2 According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , virtually all children in the United States get an RSV infection by the time they are two years old. 3 RSV represents a significant health threat for adults older than 50 years of age, with up to 180,000 hospitalizations associated with RSV infections annually in the United States . 2 Overall, in the United States , RSV accounts for up to 6.8 million outpatient visits and approximately 370,000 hospitalizations, with 24,000 deaths. 4 About Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. Enanta is using its robust, chemistry-driven approach and drug discovery capabilities to become a leader in the discovery and development of small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases. In virology, Enanta’s clinical programs are focused on the development of first-in-disease and best-in-disease treatments for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The Company’s immunology pipeline aims to develop treatments for inflammatory diseases by targeting key drivers of the type 2 immune response, with KIT, STAT6 and MRGPRX2 inhibition. Glecaprevir, a protease inhibitor discovered by Enanta, is part of the only treatment approved for curing both acute and chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and is sold by AbbVie in numerous countries under the tradenames MAVYRET® (U.S.) and MAVIRET® (ex-U.S.) (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir). A portion of Enanta’s royalties from HCV products developed under its collaboration with AbbVie contribute ongoing funding to Enanta’s operations. Please visit www.enanta.com for more information. Forward Looking Statements This press release contains forward-looking statements, including statements with respect to the Phase 2b/3 study of zelicapavir and the timeline and prospects for advancement of zelicapavir for the treatment of RSV. Statements that are not historical facts are based on management’s current expectations, estimates, forecasts and projections about Enanta’s business and the industry in which it operates and management’s beliefs and assumptions. The statements contained in this release are not guarantees of future performance and involve certain risks, uncertainties and assumptions, which are difficult to predict. Therefore, actual outcomes and results may differ materially from what is expressed in such forward-looking statements. Important factors and risks that may affect actual results include: clinical drug development involves a lengthy and expensive process with uncertain timelines and uncertain outcomes, the Phase 2b portion of Enanta’s Phase 2b/3 trial of zelicapavir for RSV may not support the Phase 3 portion, Enanta’s clinical trials, including its Phase 2b/3 trial, may fail to demonstrate sufficient safety and efficacy and, if that occurs, it may be unable to commercialize its product candidates on a timely basis or ever, the impact of development, regulatory and marketing efforts of others with respect to vaccines and competitive treatments for RSV; the discovery and development risks of Enanta’s programs in virology and immunology; Enanta’s limited clinical development experience; Enanta’s ability to partner its RSV or other programs; Enanta’s need to attract and retain senior management and key research and development personnel; Enanta’s need to obtain and maintain patent protection for its product candidates and avoid potential infringement of the intellectual property rights of others; and other risk factors described or referred to in “Risk Factors” in Enanta’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year-ended September 30, 2025, as updated by periodic reports subsequently filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Enanta cautions investors not to place undue reliance on the forward-looking statements contained in this release. news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Strengthening surveillance and testing for respiratory syncytial virus in Vietnam. On the morning of October 22nd, in Hanoi, the National Institute of Hygiene and Epidemiology organized a scientific workshop titled "Surveillance and Testing of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in Vietnam: Current Situation, Gaps, and Directions for Enhancement". Báo Quân đội Nhân dân•22/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 The workshop focused on assessing the burden of disease caused by RSV, and also discussed surveillance, testing, and solutions to improve the effectiveness of disease prevention and control in Vietnam. Dr. Ngo Duy Nghia, Head of the Department of Infectious Disease Control, National Institute of Hygiene and Epidemiology, presented his paper at the conference. Speaking at the workshop, Dr. Ngo Duy Nghia, Head of the Department of Infectious Disease Control at the National Institute of Hygiene and Epidemiology, stated that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is one of the most common causes of respiratory infections, primarily transmitted through droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces. Most children have been infected with RSV before the age of two, with infants, especially those under six months old, having a higher risk of severe illness and death. The elderly and those with underlying health conditions are also vulnerable to infection with this virus. Alarmingly, the burden of RSV-related disease worldwide remains high. According to research presented at the conference, in 2019, an estimated 33 million cases of RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections occurred globally in children under 5 years old, including 3.6 million hospitalizations and approximately 101,400 deaths. Notably, 46% of RSV-related deaths occurred in children under 6 months old, highlighting the severity of the disease for young children. Dr. Vu Ngoc Long, representing the Department of Disease Prevention ( Ministry of Health ), presented a paper at the conference. In Vietnam, research results also show that RSV is a significant factor in cases of respiratory tract infections in hospitalized children. According to studies cited by the reporter, the detection rate of RSV in hospitalized children at Children's Hospital 1 was 26%, and at the Tropical Diseases Hospital it was 24%. A study on children under 2 years old with acute bronchiolitis also recorded RSV infection in 50.65% of cases. Sign Up Today My Account Dashboard Profile Saved items Logout Home About Us Contact Us Board of Directors Donate Our Donors Advertise Corrections Subscription Services Submission Forms Newsletters Privacy Policy Terms of Use News Loudoun Leesburg Education Public Safety Towns Politics Business Giving Back Obituaries Get Out Loudoun Calendar Calendar Happenings Artist Profiles Venues Taste Loudoun Moment Add Your Event Calendar Opinion Editorials Columnists Letters to the Editor Reader's Polls Sports Public Notices Donate Loudoun Now Voice Get The App Newsletter Signup Share This Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Advertorial How to Protect Babies from RSV Oct 27, 2026 10 hrs ago 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save (StatePoint) Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, infects people of all ages, however, it can be dangerous for babies and some young children. As many as 80,000 children under 5 in the United States are hospitalized each year due to the disease. Fortunately, there are proven-effective methods to significantly reduce severe illness for babies. Here’s what the American Lung Association, with support from Sanofi, wants caregivers, parents, and expectant parents to know about protecting their babies from RSV: RSV is common. RSV is so common that by age 2, nearly 100% of children will be infected. Most people, including infants, develop only mild symptoms, like that of a common cold. For some though, RSV can be severe and even life threatening. All infants are at increased risk for severe illness. If a child does come down with RSV and they are having difficulty breathing, not drinking enough, or their symptoms are getting worse, it’s time to seek emergency care. RSV season is now. The RSV season typically starts in the fall and peaks in the winter in the United States. Because of this, parents should take action to protect their infants, especially those under eight months old and those born throughout the entire season. There are multiple ways to protect infants. It is recommended that all babies be protected from severe RSV by one of these two immunization options during RSV season (most babies do not need both): • A preventive antibody for infants younger than 8 months old and born during or entering their first RSV season. Preventive antibodies are not vaccines, but rather proteins that mimic the immune system’s naturally produced antibodies to help fight off harmful viruses. A single dose provides protection for at least five months and begins working right away. Young children between 8 and 19 months at increased risk for severe RSV symptoms, including children with chronic lung disease, are recommended to receive an RSV preventive antibody. • An RSV vaccination received during weeks 32 through 36 weeks of pregnancy. Protection lasts about six months after birth. These methods are effective. Marking the second RSV season with widespread availability of both preventive options, 2025-2026 resulted in a reduced risk of severe RSV and RSV-related hospitalizations in infants. A Centers for Disease Control and Prevention analysis of RSV hospitalization rates among two surveillance groups from October 2024 through February 2025 found hospitalization rates 45% and 52% lower for infants 0-2 months during peak RSV season (December through February) and 28% and 43% lower for those 0-7 months old, compared to pre-pandemic (2018) rates. Preventive actions can also help. RSV is spread person-to-person via coughing and sneezing, by touching objects that have the virus on them, and by direct contact, like when kissing a baby while sick with RSV. That is why parents and caregivers of babies are also encouraged to follow everyday preventive actions like: • Avoiding close contact with sick people • Covering coughs and sneezes with a tissue • Washing hands often with soap and water for 20 seconds • Cleaning frequently touched surfaces • Staying home and avoiding close contact with others when sick • Avoiding shared cups, bottles or toys For more information and to learn more, visit Lung.org/rsv. Severe RSV can be unpredictable. As the leading cause of hospitalization in infants, it is vital for parents and caregivers to take RSV seriously, and to protect their babies. ***** Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save × Post a comment as anonymous Emoticons [smile] [beam] [wink] [sad] [cool] [innocent] [rolleyes] [whistling] [lol] [huh] [tongue] [love] [sleeping] [yawn] [unsure] [angry] [blink] [crying] [ohmy] [scared] [sleep] [sneaky] [tongue_smile] [thumbdown] [thumbup] [censored] [happybirthday] [ban] [spam] [offtopic] [batman] [ninja] [pirate] [alien] Comment Text × Report × Watch this discussion. Clinical Daily News CDC: Almost 1 in 10 adults with RSV died at hospital or within 30 days of discharge Foster Stubbs (Photo: South_agency/Getty Images) October 26, 2026 Share › Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share by Email Print (Photo: South_agency/Getty Images) A total of 8.6% of adults hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) died during hospitalization or within the 30 days after they were discharged, according to CDC analysis of eight RSV seasons reported at the IDWeek annual meeting. The analysis examined data from 18,301 adults hospitalized with RSV at some point between 2014 and 2024; they were included in the CDC’s Respiratory Virus Hospitalization Surveillance Network (RESP-NET). Illness attributable to RSV infection can range from mild cold-like signs and symptoms to pneumonia or bronchiolitis. RSV vaccination in adults began during the 2023-2024 season, and the CDC recommends a one-time, single dose of any of three Food and Drug Administration-licensed vaccines for all adults ages 75 or older, or those age 50-74 who are at greater risk of severe RSV. The percentage of adults hospitalized with RSV who died peaked at 9.7% in 2015-2016 and bottomed out at 7.4% in 2018-2019. Of the 1,565 deaths reported during hospitalization or within 30 days of discharge, 812 occurred in the hospital and 753 came within 30 days post-discharge. Among those who died after discharge, 286 were discharged to hospice. Meanwhile, 467 (2.6%) people died after being discharged to somewhere other than hospice. “We think [people being discharged to somewhere other than hospice] is the most concerning, as these patients were likely discharged home or to some higher level of care — but they were probably not expected to die within a month of the hospitalization with RSV infection,” Michael Melgar, MD, of the CDC in Atlanta told MedPage Today. “These preliminary results speak to an increased mortality risk in the immediate post-hospitalization period and support overarching prevention messaging about prioritizing recommended RSV vaccination for eligible adults.” Top Stories View All News Senators allege abuse, deficiencies will be missed under Risk-Based Surveys News Also in the News for Wednesday, Oct. 28 News Why CMS nursing home chief says more past noncompliance citations may be coming Editors' Picks View All Understaffed but ineligible: Is CMS missing a chance to lift up safety-net nursing homes? analysis.time: The CDC analysis of eight RSV seasons reported at the IDWeek annual meeting, with the percentage of deaths peaking at 9.7% in 2015-2016 and bottoming out at 7.4% in 2018-2019. The study included data from 2014 to 2024.
analysis.location_and_population: The analysis examined data from 18,301 adults hospitalized with RSV in the United States between 2014 and 2024, as part of the CDC’s Respiratory Virus Hospitalization Surveillance Network (RESP-NET).
analysis.event: The CDC reported that 8.6% of adults hospitalized with RSV died during hospitalization or within 30 days of discharge, based on analysis of eight RSV seasons. This includes 812 deaths during hospitalization and 753 deaths within 30 days post-discharge.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Of the 1,565 deaths reported, 286 were discharged to hospice, while 467 (2.6%) died after being discharged to other locations. The CDC highlighted the increased mortality risk in the post-hospitalization period and emphasized the importance of RSV vaccination for eligible adults.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC presented these preliminary results at the IDWeek annual meeting, supporting prevention messaging about RSV vaccination. The findings are based on surveillance data and are considered preliminary.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC reported that 8.6% of adults hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) died during hospitalization or within 30 days of discharge, based on an analysis of eight RSV seasons presented at the IDWeek annual meeting. The study, which included data from 18,301 adults hospitalized with RSV between 2014 and 2024, found that the mortality rate peaked at 9.7% in the 2015-2016 season and dropped to 7.4% in 2018-2019. Of the 1,565 deaths, 812 occurred in the hospital and 753 within 30 days post-discharge. The CDC emphasized that the risk of death in the post-hospitalization period is significant, particularly for those not discharged to hospice, and called for prioritizing RSV vaccination for eligible adults. These findings are considered preliminary and support broader prevention efforts.

They can cause symptoms ranging from mild to severe, especially in young children, older adults, and those with weakened immune systems. Despite some overlap in symptoms, these viruses are caused by different pathogens and require distinct approaches to treatment and prevention. Awareness of their differences is crucial for effective management and care, especially during peak infection seasons. Below, Doctronic explains how to tell the difference between RSV and the flu. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza (flu) share similar symptoms but affect people differently. Understanding the key differences helps in seeking timely and appropriate care. Early recognition of symptoms can prevent complications, especially in vulnerable populations. Knowing when to consult a healthcare provider is crucial for recovery and safety. What Is RSV? Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a common virus that infects the respiratory tract. It is especially known for causing bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants and young children. Most healthy adults experience mild cold-like symptoms, but RSV can lead to serious illness in vulnerable groups. The virus is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes. It can survive on surfaces for several hours, making it easy for the virus to spread in crowded environments like daycare centers and schools. RSV infections typically peak during the colder months, and while many children will contract RSV by their second birthday, most will recover without requiring hospitalization. For some, particularly those with pre-existing health conditions, RSV can lead to severe respiratory distress. Healthcare providers often recommend supportive care, such as hydration and fever management, to help alleviate symptoms. In recent years, research has focused on developing vaccines and treatments to reduce the impact of RSV, especially for high-risk populations. What Is the Flu? Influenza, commonly called the flu, is caused by influenza viruses that infect the nose, throat, and sometimes the lungs. It tends to cause more systemic symptoms like high fever, body aches, and fatigue. The flu can also lead to complications such as pneumonia and worsening of chronic health conditions. Unlike RSV, the flu can mutate rapidly, leading to different strains each season, which is why annual vaccinations are recommended to provide the best protection against the most prevalent strains. The flu virus spreads in similar ways to RSV, through respiratory droplets and contaminated surfaces. Symptoms usually appear suddenly and can be severe, often leading individuals to seek medical attention. Antiviral medications can be effective in reducing the duration and severity of flu symptoms if taken early in the course of the illness. Public health campaigns emphasize the importance of vaccination, hand hygiene, and staying home when sick to prevent the spread of the flu, particularly among vulnerable populations such as the elderly and those with chronic health issues. Key Symptom Differences Between RSV and Flu While RSV and the flu share some symptoms, there are subtle differences that can help you tell them apart. Common Symptoms of RSV Runny nose and nasal congestion Coughing and wheezing Fever, usually mild to moderate Rapid or troubled breathing, especially in infants Decreased appetite and irritability in young children Common Symptoms of the Flu Sudden onset of high fever Severe muscle and body aches Chills and sweats Fatigue and weakness lasting several days Dry cough and sore throat How Symptoms Progress RSV symptoms often start with a runny nose and mild cough, then can progress to wheezing and breathing difficulties. The flu usually hits fast with a high fever and intense body aches, followed by respiratory symptoms. Recognizing these patterns can guide you in seeking the right care. Who Is Most at Risk? Both RSV and flu can affect anyone, but certain groups face higher risks of severe illness. High-Risk Groups for RSV Infants, especially those under 6 months Premature babies Older adults, particularly those over 65 years old People with chronic lung or heart conditions Individuals with weakened immune systems High-Risk Groups for Flu Young children under 5 years, especially under 2 years Adults over 65 years Pregnant women People with chronic illnesses like asthma, diabetes, or heart disease Residents of nursing homes or long-term care facilities Diagnosis and When to Seek Care Because symptoms overlap, professional diagnosis is important. Testing can confirm whether RSV or flu is causing the illness, guiding treatment decisions. How Diagnosis Is Made Doctors often use nasal or throat swabs to test for RSV and flu viruses. These tests can deliver results quickly, sometimes within minutes. If you or your child is experiencing severe symptoms or worsening breathing, prompt medical evaluation is essential. Treatment Options for RSV and Flu Treatment varies depending on the virus and the severity of symptoms. Managing RSV There is no specific antiviral treatment for RSV in most cases. Care focuses on relieving symptoms and supporting breathing. This may include: Using a humidifier to ease breathing Ensuring adequate fluid intake Monitoring oxygen levels in severe cases Hospitalization for infants or those with respiratory distress Managing the Flu Antiviral medications can reduce the severity and duration of flu if started early. Supportive care includes rest, hydration, and fever management. Vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent the flu each season. When to Contact a Doctor Difficulty breathing or rapid breathing High fever that does not respond to medication Persistent chest pain or wheezing Dehydration signs like dry mouth or little urine output Symptoms worsening after initial improvement Preventing RSV and Flu Prevention strategies overlap but have some differences. Preventing RSV Frequent hand washing Avoiding close contact with sick individuals Cleaning and disinfecting surfaces Limiting the exposure of infants to crowded places during the RSV season Vaccine for eligible individuals Preventing the Flu Annual flu vaccination for everyone over 6 months Good respiratory hygiene, like covering coughs and sneezes Staying home when sick to avoid spreading the virus Take the Next Step Toward Respiratory Care Knowing the differences between RSV and the flu can help you respond quickly and appropriately. Both illnesses can be serious, but early recognition and care improve outcomes. Frequently Asked Questions Can RSV and flu occur at the same time? Yes, it is possible to be infected with both RSV and flu simultaneously, which can increase the severity of symptoms. Medical evaluation is important if symptoms worsen suddenly. Is there a vaccine for RSV? Yes, there is a vaccine for certain eligible individuals. How long do RSV and flu symptoms last? RSV symptoms typically last one to two weeks, while flu symptoms often resolve within a week, but fatigue can linger longer. When should children with RSV or flu see a doctor? Seek medical care if your child has difficulty breathing, a high fever not responding to medication, dehydration, or worsening symptoms. Can adults get severe RSV infections? Yes, older adults and those with chronic health conditions can experience severe RSV infections requiring medical attention. news.content_title: RSV cases surge among infants as seasonal changes bring coughing and breathing risks
news.content: AI Automated Translation. Font Size A A A A A Share AI Automated Translation. Stock Finance Industry Living Economy Tech Future theBio Entertainment RSV cases surge among infants as seasonal changes bring coughing and breathing risks Home > theBio RSV cases surge among infants as seasonal changes bring coughing and breathing risks By Hong Hyojin 2:15 p.m. Oct 23, 2026 Week 42: 60 RSV infection hospitalizations among ages 0–6 Symptoms similar to the common cold... potential for worsening into pneumonia In severe cases, symptoms such as cyanosis, dehydration, and respiratory distress may occur Number of hospitalized patients with RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) based on Weeks 39–42 / Graphic by Lee Ji-hye Recently, the number of hospitalized patients with RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) infection has been showing an increasing trend, particularly among infants and young children. While RSV symptoms are similar to those of the common cold, it can cause severe infections such as pneumonia in infants under 6 to 12 months of age, making prevention a critical aspect of this respiratory infectious disease. According to KDCA sentinel surveillance statistics released on the 23rd, the number of domestic RSV hospitalizations stood at 65 as of Week 42 (the 11th–17), with patients aged 0 to 6 (60 cases) accounting for the largest share. The number of hospitalizations due to RSV infection has been steadily increasing since Week 39 (the 20th–26). RSV is a common respiratory virus in infants and young children, typically circulating from autumn through the following spring. In South Korea, the epidemic usually begins in October, with patient numbers rising until March of the following year. Although symptoms resemble those of a general cold, infants under 12 months of age with weak immune systems may experience worsening conditions, such as bronchiolitis or pneumonia, which are lower respiratory tract infections. In severe cases, respiratory distress may necessitate hospitalization for treatment. In babies infected with RSV, distinct rattling sounds from phlegm and wheezing breathing typically become apparent within 3 to 4 days after the onset of coughing. Symptoms can worsen, leading to frequent nighttime coughing that prevents proper sleep or causing vomiting. Adults, including pregnant women, may experience no symptoms or only mild cold-like symptoms even when infected with RSV; however, caution is required as they may unknowingly transmit the infection to vulnerable infants. Hong Ju-hee, a pediatric specialist at H+ Yangji Hospital, emphasized, “Infants have difficulty expelling phlegm, so their conditions can deteriorate rapidly.” She added, “Caregivers should monitor for signs such as retractions (inward pulling of the skin below the ribs), dehydration (no urine output for more than 6 hours), and cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the lips and extremities).” RSV can be transmitted not only through droplets released during coughing or sneezing but also via contact with multiple pathways, such as hands or toys contaminated with the virus. In particular, postpartum care facilities where mothers and newborns live together face a risk of cluster infections if even one infected individual is present. Recently, there was a case at a postpartum care facility in Jeju where 20 people, including newborns and facility staff, were infected with RSV. To reduce the risk of hospitalization, preventive antibody injections can be considered. RSV antibody injections work by directly administering pre-formed antibodies to enhance defense against the virus. Research results are emerging indicating that lower respiratory tract infection-related hospitalizations have decreased in South Korea following the introduction of RSV preventive antibodies. Long-acting RSV preventive antibodies are known to provide approximately 5 months of protective effect with a single dose. At home, it is advisable to maintain indoor humidity at 50–60% and avoid cold air as much as possible. RSV reinfection is common, and infants with underlying conditions, such as preterm birth or chronic heart and lung diseases, are at high risk of developing severe illness. Older adults aged 65 and above may also progress to pneumonia upon RSV infection, necessitating caution regarding transmission within families. Lee Jin-cheol, Lee Deul-byeong-won (Prof.) of Seongbuk Ouria, stated, “RSV infection is highly transmissible, with most children being infected at least once before their second birthday.” He added, “Since treatment focuses on symptomatic relief of respiratory symptoms rather than specific therapy to eliminate the virus itself, preventing severe disease is paramount.” "This article was translated using AI and may differ slightly from the original." 1. Click Here Local News Manitoba's RSV vaccine rules leave some seniors seeking answers Cory Knutt, PortageOnline.com | Sunday, Oct 25 2026, 12:00 PM Share: Copied! A flu vaccine is prepared for administration as Manitobans are encouraged to get their seasonal influenza shots. Photo submitted/Rhonda Kitchen Article continues below advertisement ↴ Manitobans aged 80 and older who qualify for a free respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine cannot currently receive it at pharmacies, leaving some seniors looking for other options to access the immunization. The provincial program took effect Oct. 1, expanding access to the RSV vaccine for people aged 80 and older. Rhonda Kitchen, owner and pharmacist at Hills Drug Store, said her pharmacy has been receiving calls from patients confused about where they can get the free vaccine. Kitchen said information in the provincial letter sent to eligible seniors indicates they can receive the RSV vaccine alongside their flu and COVID-19 shots, but does not clearly explain that pharmacies cannot administer the publicly funded RSV vaccine under current regulations. “Unfortunately, it doesn't state that that cannot be at the pharmacy,” Kitchen said. RSV vaccine requires another provider Kitchen said pharmacists can administer the RSV vaccine with a doctor's prescription, but patients must pay for it in that situation. “Currently, the regulations do not allow pharmacists to provide that vaccine unless we have a prescription order from the doctor and the patients are paying for it,” she noted. That differs from the provincial program, which provides the vaccine free of charge to eligible seniors. “It does need to be done at either one of the flu clinics in their local area or at public health or through their doctor's office,” Kitchen commented. Related stories: Portage la Prairie families gather as Hill’s Drugstore marks 125 years 'Frustrated' pharmacy owner searches for fix after week-long cell phone outage Listen to this news story on the radio: Country 93 / Mix 96 / CFRY 920 Kitchen said her pharmacy has been fielding questions from patients trying to understand the difference. She recommends checking the information included with the provincial letter or contacting public health for guidance. Pharmacies continue to offer other vaccines Although pharmacies cannot currently administer the publicly funded RSV vaccine, Kitchen said they can provide several other vaccines at no cost to eligible patients. These include seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccines, as well as the updated pneumococcal vaccine for eligible adults aged 65 and older. Pharmacists can also provide tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis boosters when patients are due for one, generally every 10 years. Click Here Local News Manitoba's RSV vaccine rules leave some seniors seeking answers Cory Knutt, PortageOnline.com | Sunday, Oct 25 2026, 12:00 PM Share: Copied! A flu vaccine is prepared for administration as Manitobans are encouraged to get their seasonal influenza shots. Photo submitted/Rhonda Kitchen Article continues below advertisement ↴ Manitobans aged 80 and older who qualify for a free respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine cannot currently receive it at pharmacies, leaving some seniors looking for other options to access the immunization. The provincial program took effect Oct. 1, expanding access to the RSV vaccine for people aged 80 and older. Rhonda Kitchen, owner and pharmacist at Hills Drug Store, said her pharmacy has been receiving calls from patients confused about where they can get the free vaccine. Kitchen said information in the provincial letter sent to eligible seniors indicates they can receive the RSV vaccine alongside their flu and COVID-19 shots, but does not clearly explain that pharmacies cannot administer the publicly funded RSV vaccine under current regulations. “Unfortunately, it doesn't state that that cannot be at the pharmacy,” Kitchen said. RSV vaccine requires another provider Kitchen said pharmacists can administer the RSV vaccine with a doctor's prescription, but patients must pay for it in that situation. “Currently, the regulations do not allow pharmacists to provide that vaccine unless we have a prescription order from the doctor and the patients are paying for it,” she noted. That differs from the provincial program, which provides the vaccine free of charge to eligible seniors. “It does need to be done at either one of the flu clinics in their local area or at public health or through their doctor's office,” Kitchen commented. Related stories: Portage la Prairie families gather as Hill’s Drugstore marks 125 years 'Frustrated' pharmacy owner searches for fix after week-long cell phone outage Listen to this news story on the radio: Country 93 / Mix 96 / CFRY 920 Kitchen said her pharmacy has been fielding questions from patients trying to understand the difference. She recommends checking the information included with the provincial letter or contacting public health for guidance. Pharmacies continue to offer other vaccines Although pharmacies cannot currently administer the publicly funded RSV vaccine, Kitchen said they can provide several other vaccines at no cost to eligible patients. These include seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccines, as well as the updated pneumococcal vaccine for eligible adults aged 65 and older. Pharmacists can also provide tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis boosters when patients are due for one, generally every 10 years. Where seniors can get help Kitchen recommends that people with questions about their RSV vaccine eligibility or where to receive the publicly funded dose contact Manitoba Public Health at 204-856-2040. Dr. Alex Summers, medical officer of health with the Middlesex-London Health Unit, was photographed on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026. Matthew Daldalian/The London Free Press By Brian Williams October 27, 2026 at 12:28 p.m. As Southwestern Ontario and the rest of the province gets set to enter respiratory virus season, public health offices are preparing for the spread of illnesses, including COVID-19 and influenza. Here are some things to know about the risks ahead. WHICH RESPIRATORY VIRUSES ARE MOST CLOSELY MONITORED? The respiratory illnesses most closely monitored by the Middlesex-London Health Unit are influenza, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), said Alex Summers, the health unit’s medical officer of health. Summers said there are other “common cold respiratory viruses” that will circulate over respiratory illness season, but those are the “big three” the public health office monitors. Send Close Pediatric Infections Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on X Email Article Copy Article Url Print OCTOBER 23, 2026 IDWeek 2026 RSV-B Lineage Emerges as Standout in Severe Pediatric Disease By Anna Tsioulias Young children infected with certain respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) subgroup B lineages experienced greater disease severity than those infected with RSV-A, according to a study presented at IDWeek 2026, in Washington, D.C. Source: Adobe. The biggest potential culprit? RSV-B lineage B.D.E.1. Related Content RSV Vaccination Shows Effectiveness at Year 3 A new study has found that vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains effective three years ... This Year’s U.S. Measles Cases Soar Beyond 4,000 The United States has identified 4,080 confirmed measles cases in 2026, as of CDC data updated on Oct. 8. Starting HPV Vaccine at Age 9 or 10 Raises Series Completion by 13 Starting the HPV vaccine series younger substantially increased the share of children who began and finished the ... The findings shed new light on a longstanding debate regarding the relative virulence of RSV antigenic subgroups. Although both RSV-A and RSV-B are established players in severe pediatric respiratory disease, prior studies have yielded conflicting results on whether differences in viral glycoproteins, including the fusion (F) and attachment (G) proteins, influence clinical severity. “We actually initially thought RSV-A was more pathogenic than RSV-B,” explained Kim El Haddad, MD, a pediatric infectious diseases physician at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, in Washington, D.C. “These new findings help clarify with very statistically significant results that the lineage B was associated with worse outcomes, although the fact that this study had more RSV-B than RSV-A cases (216 vs. 129) might affect precision.” In a prospective study spanning seven respiratory seasons (2015-2021), investigators at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, in Memphis, Tennessee, collected nasal swabs from 345 previously healthy children younger than 2 years of age: 22% with mild (outpatient) and 78% with moderate to severe (inpatient) RSV infection. After whole-genome sequencing, significant differences emerged across six RSV lineages with regard to disease severity scores (P=0.01), pediatric ICU admissions (P<0.0001), duration of oxygen supplementation (P=0.04), oxygen delivery methods (P<0.0001), and hospital length of stay (P=0.03). B.D.E.1 (n=61) was associated with particularly severe clinical outcomes, with nearly three-fourths of infected children requiring PICU admission. However, Dr. El Haddad, who was not involved with the research, noted that the changing distribution of RSV lineages across respiratory seasons could complicate interpretation, especially considering disruptions in viral circulation during the COVID-19 pandemic. “During peak COVID times, isolation measures created what we call an immunity debt, as many children were not exposed to RSV,” Dr. El Haddad told Infectious Disease Special Edition. “When restrictions eased in 2021, we saw a surge in B.D.E.1 infections. I wonder whether this lack of previous exposure contributed to a stronger inflammatory response with elevated cytokine levels and ultimately more severe disease. “I would also be interested in knowing whether viral loads differed between RSV-A and RSV-B infections, as reflected by cycle threshold values. A higher viral burden could contribute to both the more pronounced inflammatory response and greater disease severity observed with certain RSV-B lineages.” Looking beyond differences in clinical severity, the investigators uncovered distinct genomic and inflammatory profiles among RSV subgroups. More specifically, RSV-B showed greater sequence variability across F, G, and M2-2 proteins, raising questions about potential implications for RSV immunoprophylaxis. Dr. El Haddad noted that nirsevimab (Beyfortus, Sanofi/AstraZeneca) and clesrovimab (Enflonsia, Merck) target the F protein, but whether the observed genetic variation influences monoclonal antibody effectiveness remains unknown; however, she considered a clinically meaningful impact unlikely. RSV-B infections were also linked with a more pronounced mucosal inflammatory response, with age-adjusted analyses identifying 22 cytokines at significantly higher concentrations than in RSV-A infections (P<0.01). These cytokines formed two distinct clusters: one involving innate immune activation and interleukin-1 signaling, the other with chemotaxis and cellular stress pathways. Of importance, previous RSV exposure and the associated immune response could potentially affect cytokine profiles and disease severity during subsequent infections, according to Dr. El Haddad. “As the authors didn’t mention it, I am interested to know whether any children had prior RSV infections. If prior infection was not accounted for, it could represent a potential confounder.” Dr. El Haddad reported no relevant financial disclosures.
